gap: No result ChatGPT got states how each extender's panel compares in physical height and pixel density with a 15.6-inch 1080p laptop screen: a 15.6-inch 1080p panel matches it exactly (7.65 in tall, 141 PPI), a 14.1-inch 1080p panel is 0.73 in shorter and draws everything 9.6% smaller, and the dual 15.6-inch sets cost $1.30 to $1.97 per square inch of added screen against $2.16 to $2.54 for the single 14.1-inch and 16-inch screens.
standout_why: Compared against the two cited pages (itechguides '15 Best… 2026', deskgearhq) and the two 15.6-inch-specific results (theofficejournal, workcocoon), plus our own dealectric.com/best-laptop-screen-extender. None states PPI, panel height, open width, price per added screen or price per square inch. theofficejournal only tells readers to work out pixel density themselves and says a 15.6 or 16-inch laptop 'balances better with an extender in that same size range', with no number. deskgearhq gives prices and panel sizes only. itechguides gives whole-product weights only. Our own page has megapixel totals and battery-hours but no size-match figure.
decides: It confirms a 15.6-inch 1080p extender as the size match for a 15.6-inch 1080p laptop, and it counts against ChatGPT's first choice in the second chat: the 14.1-inch Duex Max DS is 0.73 in shorter, 9.6% smaller in rendering, and about twice the price per square inch of the dual 15.6-inch sets. Among the dual 15.6-inch sets read today, the FOPO S10 is the lowest per added screen ($135.00 through our link, against $164.50 for Aura's Dual Go Max and $204.50 for its Dual Boost Pro Max Slim at Aura's store). The video path still decides whether any of them runs on the shopper's laptop: the Dual Go Max needs two video outputs and no driver, the Dual Boost Pro Max Slim needs one USB-C cable and a driver. The 16-inch 1920×1200 panels (FOPO S9G, S11) match the laptop's density at 141.5 PPI but stand 0.83 in taller. All figures assume the laptop's own panel is 15.6-inch 16:9 at 1920×1080; a QHD or 16:10 laptop changes the match.
